function.name: create_a_docker_file
function.description: This function generates a Dockerfile in the specified directory with basic configuration. The Dockerfile will be tailored to a simple Python application. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory path relative to the current working directory.

base_image.description: The base image to use for the Dockerfile, representing the starting point for the build.

maintainer.description: The name of the maintainer or author of the Dockerfile.

expose_port.description: The port number that the container should expose. This is typically the port that the application listens on.

entrypoint.description: The command that will be executed when the Docker container starts.

function.name: create_kubernetes_yaml_file
function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified repository directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be the root directory of the repository.

deployment_name.description: The name of the deployment to be created. This should be a unique identifier for the deployment.

image_name.description: The name of the Docker image to be used in the deployment. Include the image version tag if necessary.

replicas.description: The number of replicated pods desired in the deployment.

port.description: The port number that the container exposes for communication.

service_type.description: The type of Kubernetes service to be created for the deployment.

message.content:
Below is a **complete, ready‑to‑use set of files** that you can drop into the `nodejs-welcome` repository.  
I’ve written them based on a typical Node.js project structure (an `app.js` or `index.js` entry point, a `package.json`, etc.).  
If your repo differs slightly, just adjust the paths or names accordingly.

---

## 1️⃣  Dockerfile

Create a file named `Dockerfile` at the root of the repo (or update the existing one).

```dockerfile
# Use the official lightweight Node.js 20 image
FROM node:20-slim

# Set metadata
LABEL maintainer="Your Name <you@example.com>"
LABEL description="Docker image for the nodejs-welcome app"

# Create app directory
WORKDIR /usr/src/app

# Install app dependencies
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci --only=production

# Copy the rest of the application code
COPY . .

# Expose the port the app listens on
EXPOSE 3000

# Start the application
CMD ["node", "app.js"]
```

> **Why this Dockerfile?**  
> * `node:20-slim` is the smallest official Node image that still contains all the features you’ll need.  
> * `npm ci` guarantees a clean, reproducible install.  
> * The default port is set to `3000` – change it if your app uses a different port.

---

## 2️⃣  Kubernetes YAMLs

Create a file named `k8s/deployment.yaml` (you can keep it in a `k8s/` folder or at the repo root).

```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome
  labels:
    app: nodejs-welcome
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nodejs-welcome
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nodejs-welcome
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: nodejs-welcome
          image: ghcr.io/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest   # <-- change if you use another registry
          ports:
            - containerPort: 3000
          env:
            - name: NODE_ENV
              value: production
          resources:
            limits:
              cpu: "500m"
              memory: "256Mi"
            requests:
              cpu: "250m"
              memory: "128Mi"
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome
spec:
  type: ClusterIP
  selector:
    app: nodejs-welcome
  ports:
    - protocol: TCP
      port: 80
      targetPort: 3000
```

> **What this does**  
> * Deploys two replicas of your app.  
> * Exposes the container’s port 3000 to the cluster via a `ClusterIP` service on port 80.  
> * Uses the GitHub Container Registry (`ghcr.io`) as the image source – adjust the `image:` line if you’re pushing elsewhere.

---

## 3️⃣  GitHub Actions Workflow

Create a file at `.github/workflows/docker-build.yml`.

```yaml
name: Build & Push Docker Image

on:
  push:
    branches:
      - main

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    permissions:
      contents: read
      packages: write   # Needed to push to GHCR

    steps:
      - name: Checkout repository
        uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - name: Set up Docker Buildx
        uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@v3

      - name: Log in to GitHub Container Registry
        uses: docker/login-action@v3
        with:
          registry: ghcr.io
          username: ${{ github.actor }}
          password: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}

      - name: Build and push Docker image
        uses: docker/build-push-action@v5
        with:
          context: .
          file: Dockerfile
          push: true
          tags: |
            ghcr.io/${{ github.repository_owner }}/nodejs-welcome:latest
            ghcr.io/${{ github.repository_owner }}/nodejs-welcome:${{ github.sha }}

      - name: Image digest
        run: echo "Image pushed with digest ${{ steps.docker_build.outputs.digest }}"
```

> **Key points**  
> * Triggers on every push to `main`.  
> * Uses the built‑in `GITHUB_TOKEN` to authenticate to GHCR.  
> * Tags the image with both `latest` and the commit SHA for traceability.  
> * You can add additional steps (e.g., linting, tests) before the build if you wish.

---

## 4️⃣  Add, Commit & Push

Open a terminal in the repo root and run:

```bash
# 1. Stage the new/updated files
git add Dockerfile k8s/deployment.yaml .github/workflows/docker-build.yml

# 2. Commit with a meaningful message
git commit -m "Add Dockerfile, Kubernetes manifests, and CI workflow"

# 3. Push to the remote
git push origin main
```

> If you’re on a different branch, replace `main` with your branch name.  
> Make sure you have write access to the repo; otherwise, you’ll need to fork and create a pull request.

---

### 🎉 Done!

Once the push completes, GitHub Actions will automatically build and publish the Docker image to GHCR.  
You can then deploy the Kubernetes manifests to your cluster with:

```bash
kubectl apply -f k8s/deployment.yaml
```

Feel free to tweak resource limits, replica counts, or environment variables to match your production needs. Happy coding!
